It's essentially just a motorized circular saw system with a specialized enclosure built into a table I already have a Milwaukee circular saw. I imagine I could cut part of a table out and just hook this right into it I would need to add the end blocks so that I can slide boards along the saw easily
turns.response_html:
While it sounds straightforward in theory, converting a handheld circular saw into a makeshift table saw is actually a classic woodworking project—and a notoriously dangerous one.

Yes, it is essentially a circular saw mounted upside down to a table, but the translation from handheld to stationary introduces major mechanical and safety challenges.

Here is a breakdown of why it’s trickier than it looks, and what you need to consider before cutting up a table.

1. The Biggest Obstacle: The Fence (Your "End Blocks")

A table saw is only as good as its fence (the guide you slide the board against).

  • The Precision Problem: For a table saw to work safely, the fence must be perfectly parallel to the blade. If the back of the fence is even a millimeter closer to the blade than the front, it will pinch the wood against the spinning blade.
  • The Result: This causes instant, violent kickback, firing the board back at your chest at speeds over 100 mph. Designing a DIY fence that locks down perfectly parallel every single time is often harder than mounting the saw itself.

2. Mounting and Alignment Hurdles

Getting your Milwaukee saw attached to the underside of the table requires absolute precision.

  • Squaring the Blade: The blade must be perfectly parallel to the miter slots or the edge of the table. If it’s slightly crooked, the wood will bind, resulting in burned edges or kickback.
  • Loss of Depth: When you mount a circular saw under a table, you lose the thickness of the tabletop in cutting depth. If your tabletop is $\frac{3}{4}\text{-inch}$ thick, your maximum depth of cut shrinks by that exact amount.
  • Adjustments: Changing the blade height or angle means crawling under the table to fiddle with the circular saw’s manual levers, which is clumsy and inaccurate.

3. Critical Safety Missing Pieces

Commercial table saws have safety features built into their design that handheld saws completely lack:

  • The Riving Knife / Splitter: This is a small metal plate that sits directly behind the blade. It keeps the two cut halves of the wood from pinching together. Handheld circular saws do not have these fixed in place for table use. Without one, the risk of kickback skyrocketed.
  • The Power Switch: If a piece of wood starts binding or smoking, you cannot reach under the table to let go of the circular saw trigger. You have to rig up a dedicated, easily accessible safety power switch (like a paddle switch you can hit with your knee) to cut power instantly.

If You Decide to Build It Anyway...

If you treat this as a precision engineering project rather than a quick weekend hack, people do build successful versions. Here is how to approach it safely:

  • Use a Rigid Insert Plate: Don't just screw the saw to wood. Cut a large rectangular hole in your table and mount the saw to a flat piece of $\frac{1}{4}\text{-inch}$ aluminum or thick phenolic resin sheet, then drop that plate into the table (similar to a router table setup). This preserves cutting depth and maintains flatness.
  • Build a "Splitter": You must fashion a homemade splitter just behind the blade insert to prevent wood pinching.
  • Use a Commercial Track System: Instead of relying on wooden blocks for a fence, buy a commercial T-track and build a fence that locks securely into it on both ends to ensure parallelism.

The Bottom Line

It’s entirely doable if you have the patience for meticulous alignment and building safety overrides. However, given the price of entry-level portable job site table saws on the used market, buying a secondhand commercial unit is often safer, more accurate, and saves an immense amount of fabrication time.

Exactly. You hit the nail on the head.

If you are constantly dropping the saw into the table and taking it back out to use as a handheld tool, you will have to recalibrate it every single time. It completely ruins the utility. Having a dedicated saw permanently bolted and aligned under that table is the only realistic way to make it viable.

Once it is locked down permanently, ensuring it maintains that calibration is where your mechanical design choices come into play. Here is how you can engineering-proof the build to lock in that alignment and safety.

1. The Core Alignment: The Plate Mounting System

To ensure the saw never shifts under the table from vibration or torque, do not mount the saw's shoe directly to wood. Wood expands, contracts, and compresses over time.

Instead, use a heavy-duty insert plate (like a thick aluminum router plate).

  • You permanently bolt the circular saw's metal baseplate to this aluminum sheet using machined screws and locking nuts.
  • You then cut a recessed lip into your wooden table so the aluminum plate drops in flush.
  • Because the saw is rigidly fixed to the aluminum, and the aluminum sits tightly in a fitted table recess, the blade's alignment to the table stays locked in.

2. Maintaining Fence Calibration

Since the fence has to move every time you want to make a different width cut, maintaining its parallelism is the hardest engineering challenge. Traditional wood "end blocks" clamped to the table sides are notorious for shifting.

To make it safe and repeatable, you need a mechanism that mechanically forces the fence to stay square:

  • The T-Square Style (Biesemeyer): This is what commercial saws use. The fence only locks onto the front rail of the table using a wide T-shape. Because the "T" head is held tight against a perfectly straight front bar, locking it down automatically pulls the long fence perfectly parallel to the blade.
  • The Dual-Track Rack and Pinion: A simpler DIY approach is running a standard metal T-track along both the front and back edges of the table. Your fence slides along these tracks, and you use threaded knobs to lock it down on both sides. To maintain calibration here, you just need a built-in pointer or ruler on both tracks so you can instantly verify that the front and back of the fence are set to the exact same millimeter.

3. The Vibration Problem (Loctite is Your Friend)

Circular saws vibrate intensely. Over hours of use, standard wood screws or basic nuts will back out, which introduces micro-movements to your blade angle.

  • Use Nyloc nuts (nuts with nylon inserts) or thread-locking fluid (Loctite 242) on every single bolt holding the saw to your mounting plate.
  • Build the table framework with rigid, heavy materials (like double-layered MDF or Baltic birch plywood) to damp the high-frequency vibrations of the universal motor.

4. The Final Calibration Step

Once you build a rigid system, your initial calibration is just a matter of using a precision combination square to measure the exact distance from the front of the blade to your miter slot (or table edge), and the back of the blade to the same slot. Once those two numbers match perfectly, you lock down your mounting plate.

If you've built the mounting frame rigidly enough, it shouldn't budge. You'd just need to check it with a square once every few months to make sure vibration hasn't caused the metal to fatigue or slip.

turns.prompt_text: That makes sense. I see a few Craftsman table saws for about $150. That's very reasonable. I imagine Milwaukee has similar
turns.response_html:
Actually, Milwaukee does not make a budget corded table saw. Unlike Craftsman, Ryobi, or DeWALT, Milwaukee completely moved away from entry-level corded options for this specific tool category.

Instead, they focus entirely on their premium, cordless M18 FUEL battery platform.

If you want a table saw to go with a Milwaukee tool setup, it will be a significant investment compared to a $150 used Craftsman. Here is what to expect from their lineup:

The Milwaukee Option

The main model available is the Milwaukee M18 FUEL 8-1/4 in. Table Saw. It is highly rated and packs the power of a standard 15-amp corded saw, but it is positioned as a high-end tool for professional jobsites.

  • The Price: The tool by itself (bare tool) sits around $599, and if you need the high-capacity battery and charger kit, it jumps closer to $749.
  • The Features: It uses an 8-1/4 inch blade, features a rack-and-pinion fence system (which completely solves the DIY calibration and alignment headache), and includes smart tracking features.

Budget Alternatives

If you just want a reliable, stationary machine for a garage or home workspace without breaking the bank, jumping on one of those $150 used Craftsman saws (or looking for a budget corded Ryobi or SKIL jobsite saw new for around $150–$200) is a much more practical route. You will get a 10-inch blade capacity rather than the smaller 8-1/4 inch blade on the cordless Milwaukee, giving you a deeper cut capacity for standard dimensional lumber.

Would you prefer to look into entry-level corded table saws under $200, or are you trying to keep everything on a matching battery platform?

Going with Ryobi is a fantastic choice if you want to skip the mechanical headache of a DIY build while keeping costs completely reasonable. They hit that entry-level sweet spot perfectly, offering both ultra-budget corded options and highly functional cordless options if you ever want to expand into their 18V battery platform.

Here are the most relevant Ryobi models right now based on features and budget:

1. The Budget Corded Pick: RYOBI RTS08 13 Amp 8-1/4 in. Table Saw

If your main goal is to get a functional tabletop setup for the absolute lowest cost without dealing with battery management, this is the way to go.

  • The Price: Sits right at $149, making it cheaper than a lot of used options out there.
  • Key Features: It runs a 13-Amp motor pushing 5,600 RPM. It uses an 8-1/4 inch blade, making the total unit incredibly lightweight and compact.
  • Design Note: Because it is a compact benchtop model without a stand, it's actually perfect if you still want to build a custom workbench or cabinet around it to get that massive, seamless tabletop workspace you originally envisioned.

2. The Full-Size Corded Pick: Ryobi Table Saw RTS12

If you want a traditional, full-size capacity setup that can handle thicker lumber and comes with its own support structure out of the box, step up to this model.

  • The Price: Sits right around $229.
  • Key Features: It upgrades you to a 15-Amp motor and a full 10-inch blade capacity. It also includes a steel roll cage frame and a folding stand.
  • Design Note: Users mention it has a more robust cutting capacity for thicker stock, though the fence requires a quick double-check for squareness when locking it down.

3. The Cordless Pick: 18V One+ HP Brushless 8-1/4" Table Saw Kit

If you love the idea of running a cordless setup like the premium Milwaukee option but want to keep the price down, Ryobi has a highly competitive brushless version.

  • The Price: Around $399 for the complete kit (includes two 4.0 Ah high-performance batteries and a charger).
  • Key Features: It features a rack-and-pinion blade height adjustment for smooth, precise alignment. It offers a 12-inch rip capacity to the right of the blade and weighs just under 33 lbs, making it highly portable.

A Recommendation for Your Project

If you still have that itch to build a custom shop table or enclosure, picking up the RYOBI RTS08 for $149 gives you a brilliant middle ground. You get a fully functional, safely guarded motor, arbor, and trunnion system that you can seamlessly mount flush inside a large, custom-built outfeed table. You get the fun of the fabrication project, but without any of the dangerous alignment or safety compromises.
